text: Tuberculosis (TB), commonly known as the "white death" or historically as consumption, is a contagious disease primarily caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) bacteria. It most commonly affects the lungs but can also involve other organs. Most TB infections are asymptomatic and are classified as inactive or latent tuberculosis, which is not contagious; however, a small proportion of latent infections can progress to active disease, which, if untreated, can be fatal. Typical symptoms of active TB include a chronic cough with blood-tinged mucus, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, while extrapulmonary TB presents with symptoms specific to the affected organ, such as urinary issues, neurological problems, or bone and joint pain. TB spreads through the air when people with active pulmonary TB cough, sneeze, speak, or sing, releasing infectious droplets that can remain airborne and infectious for several hours, especially in poorly ventilated areas. People with latent TB do not spread the disease, but those with weakened immune systems are at higher risk of progression to active TB. Two primary diagnostic tests are the tuberculin skin test and the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). Prevention strategies include screening high-risk individuals—such as household, workplace, and social contacts of people with active TB—early detection, treatment, and vaccination with the bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine. TB has existed since ancient times, with skeletal remains from 4000 BC and Egyptian mummies from 3000 to 2400 BC showing evidence of the disease; genetic studies indicate TB-like bacteria in Southern America around AD 140. Although Richard Morton identified pulmonary tubercles in 1689, TB was not recognized as a single disease until the 1820s, with Benjamin Marten suggesting in 1720 that consumption was caused by microbes spread through close living. René Laennec linked tubercles to pulmonary TB in 1819, and J. L. Schönlein first used the term "tuberculosis" in 1832. In 1865, Jean Antoine Villemin demonstrated TB transmission from humans to animals, confirmed by John Burdon-Sanderson in 1867 and 1868. Robert Koch identified M. tuberculosis on 24 March 1882 and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1905 for this discovery. In the 1800s, TB caused nearly 25% of all deaths in Europe, with one in four deaths in England in 1815 and one in six in France by 1918. Between 1838 and 1845, John Croghan attempted to cure TB patients in Mammoth Cave, Kentucky, but all died within a year. Hermann Brehmer opened the first TB sanatorium in 1859 in Görbersdorf. After TB was recognized as contagious in the 1880s, it was made a notifiable disease in Britain, leading to campaigns against public spitting and the establishment of sanatoria, though even under ideal conditions, 50% of patients died within five years. Koch initially believed human and cattle TB were distinct, delaying recognition of milk as a transmission route, which was later reduced through pasteurization. He introduced tuberculin in 1890, which was ineffective as a treatment but later adapted into a screening tool. World Tuberculosis Day is observed annually on 24 March, the date of Koch’s announcement. The Medical Research Council in Britain began focusing on TB research in 1913. Albert Calmette and Camille Guérin developed the BCG vaccine in 1906 using an attenuated bovine strain, first used in humans in 1921 in France, gaining widespread acceptance in the US, UK, and Germany only after World War II. In 1946, streptomycin enabled effective treatment of TB, replacing surgical methods like pneumothorax. By the 1950s, European TB mortality had dropped by about 90% due to improvements in sanitation, vaccination, and public health measures. Shortly after streptomycin was introduced in 1943, some TB strains developed resistance to standard drugs such as streptomycin, para-aminosalicylic acid, and isoniazid. Between 1970 and 1990, outbreaks of multi-drug resistant TB (MDR-TB)—resistant to two or more first-line drugs—occurred, leading the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global health emergency in 1993. Drug resistance occurs in two forms: primary, from person-to-person transmission of resistant bacteria, and secondary (acquired), which develops during treatment due to inadequate therapy, poor compliance, or low-quality drugs. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) is essential to identify resistance and guide treatment, with the WHO recommending the Xpert MTB/RIF test for rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistance detection. Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) resists rifampicin, while MDR-TB resists both rifampicin and isoniazid. Extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) resists rifampicin, isoniazid, at least one fluoroquinolone, and at least one Group A drug (bedaquiline or linezolid). Totally drug-resistant TB, lacking an official definition as of 2025, is described as resistance to all first- and second-line drugs and was first observed in 2003 in Italy, with later reports in Iran, India, and South Africa. As of 2023, 3.2% of new TB cases globally are RR-TB or MDR-TB—down from 4.0% in 2015—and among previously treated cases, the rate decreased from 25% in 2015 to 16% in 2023. MDR-TB treatment requires second-line drugs, which are less effective, more toxic, and more expensive than first-line drugs, with regimens lasting up to two years compared to six months for standard treatment. In the UK in 2013, standard TB treatment cost was estimated at £5,000, while MDR-TB treatment ranged from £50,000 to £70,000. In low-income countries, MDR-TB severely impacts families, affecting income, mental health, and social well-being. A common misconception is that TB is solely a lung disease with coughing; it can affect many organs, including the pleura, central nervous system, lymphatic system, genitourinary system, bones, and joints. Disseminated TB, or miliary TB, accounts for about 10% of extrapulmonary cases. The MTB bacterium is small, aerobic, nonmotile, divides every 16 to 20 hours, and has a complex, lipid-rich cell wall that contributes to its drug resistance and ability to survive in dry conditions and weak disinfectants. The M. tuberculosis complex includes other TB-causing species: M. bovis (now rare due to pasteurized milk), M. africanum (significant in parts of Africa), M. canettii (rare, limited to the Horn of Africa), and M. microti (rare in humans, mainly in immunocompromised individuals). Other mycobacteria, such as M. avium complex and M. kansasii, cause lung disease resembling TB and are classified as nontuberculous mycobacteria, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. Environmental risk factors, including overcrowding, poor ventilation, air pollution, tobacco smoke, and occupational dust exposure, increase the risk of TB infection. Close, prolonged, or frequent contact with people with active TB—such as healthcare workers or children with infected family members—is a major risk factor, while latent TB infection does not lead to transmission.

Tuberculosis (TB) spreads when a person with active TB coughs, speaks, or sings, releasing tiny airborne droplets containing *M. tuberculosis* bacteria. These droplets can be inhaled by others nearby, leading to infection, and may remain airborne and infectious for several hours, especially in poorly ventilated areas. Risk factors for TB include exposure to droplets from people with active TB, as well as environmental and health-related factors that weaken the immune system. Prolonged, frequent, or close contact with individuals who have active TB—such as healthcare workers or children with an infected family member—is a high-risk factor, while people with latent TB are not considered contagious. Environmental factors like overcrowding, poor ventilation, and close proximity to an infected person increase exposure risk. Additional environmental risks include air pollution, tobacco smoke, and occupational exposure to dust or particulates. The most significant global risk factor for developing active TB is concurrent HIV infection; in 2023, 6.1% of new TB cases were also HIV-positive, with a particularly high burden in Sub-Saharan Africa. Among those without HIV, about 5–15% develop active TB over their lifetime, compared to 30% of those co-infected with HIV, who are estimated 16 times more likely to develop active TB, making it the leading cause of death among people with HIV. Immune-suppressing medications, such as those used in chemotherapy, post-organ transplant, or for lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, also increase risk. Other risk factors include heavy alcohol use, diabetes mellitus, silicosis, tobacco smoking, recreational drug use, severe kidney disease, head and neck cancer, and low body weight. Children, especially those under five, are at higher risk due to underdeveloped immune systems. TB infection begins when *M. tuberculosis* is inhaled into the lungs and reaches the alveoli, where it is engulfed by alveolar macrophages. The macrophage engulfs the bacterium, trapping it in a phagosome that fuses with a lysosome to form a phagolysosome, where digestive enzymes destroy the invader. However, *M. tuberculosis* can inhibit phagosome maturation and prevent fusion with lysosomes, allowing it to survive and replicate within the macrophage, eventually destroying the host cell and releasing new bacteria. Macrophages, epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, and fibroblasts then aggregate to form a granuloma, which contains and isolates the bacteria without destroying them. Granulomas are most common in the lungs but can occur elsewhere; as long as the infection remains contained, there are no symptoms and the infection is latent. If the immune system fails to control the infection, active TB develops, causing damage to the lungs and other organs. If bacteria enter the bloodstream from damaged tissue, they spread throughout the body, forming multiple tiny white tubercles—known as miliary tuberculosis—common in young children and those with HIV, with a high fatality rate (about 30%) even with treatment. In many cases, tissue destruction and necrosis are balanced by healing and fibrosis, resulting in scarring and cavities filled with caseous necrotic material. During active disease, some cavities connect to airways, allowing the coughing up of bacteria-laden material that can spread infection. Treatment with antibiotics kills the bacteria and allows healing, with affected areas eventually replaced by scar tissue. Diagnosis is often difficult due to slow, non-specific symptoms such as cough, fatigue, and fever. The definitive diagnosis of pulmonary TB requires bacterial culture from sputum, though this is slow and does not detect latent TB. Extra-pulmonary TB is harder to diagnose due to limited sample access. Immune-based tests like the Mantoux skin test (involving intradermal injection of tuberculin antigen, read after 48–72 hours) and the Interferon Gamma Release Assay (IGRA), which measures interferon-gamma release from white blood cells in response to TB antigens, are used; IGRA is more reliable and avoids false positives from BCG vaccination but may give false positives for related bacteria. Chest X-rays may show infiltrates or scarring suggestive of TB, but these can be mimicked by other lung diseases and do not detect extrapulmonary or recent infections. Definitive diagnosis is achieved by detecting *M. tuberculosis* in specimens such as sputum, pus, cerebrospinal fluid, or tissue via fluorescence microscopy or culture, which can take weeks. Rapid tests like nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), including the Xpert MTB/RIF system endorsed by WHO in December 2010, and adenosine deaminase testing support faster diagnosis. Urine PCR is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosing urogenital TB. Antibody-based blood tests are not recommended due to lack of specificity and sensitivity. Prevention strategies include treating both active and latent TB and vaccinating at-risk children. Latent TB is not infectious but should be treated to prevent progression to active pulmonary TB. Active TB patients should be segregated and placed on anti-TB regimens; after about two weeks of effective treatment, they are generally no longer contagious, though full treatment—typically six months—is essential. The only available vaccine as of 2021 is BCG, administered intradermally to children under five, which reduces infection risk by 20% and the risk of progression to active disease by nearly 60%, but is ineffective in adults. In areas with low TB prevalence, BCG is given only to high-risk children, while in high-burden countries, a single dose is given soon after birth. Historically, TB was known to be caused by a bacillus spread via coughed phlegm, dried into dust and inhaled, with milk being a known transmission route. Prevention measures included ventilation, nutritious food, boiling milk, and inspecting meat. In Britain, TB was made a notifiable disease, and campaigns to stop public spitting and place the infected poor in sanatoria were implemented; similar efforts occurred in the U.S. The WHO declared TB a "global health emergency" in 1993 and launched the Stop TB Partnership’s Global Plan in 2006, aiming to save 14 million lives by 2015, though targets were not met due to rising HIV-associated TB and multi-drug resistant TB. In 2014, the WHO adopted the "End TB" strategy, aiming to reduce TB incidence by 80% and deaths by 90% by 2030, with a 20% incidence and 35% death reduction target by 2020. By 2020, only a 9% global reduction in incidence was achieved (19% in Europe, 16% in Africa), and deaths declined by only 14% (31% in Europe, 19% in Africa), missing the 2020 milestones. Treatment and prevention targets were also not met, with only 6.3 million people receiving TB prevention treatment instead of the 30 million target. The goal of TB elimination is hindered by the lack of rapid testing, short and effective treatment courses, and a completely effective vaccine. TB treatment uses first-line drugs—isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol—which are preferred due to effectiveness and fewer side effects. Second-line drugs are used when resistance develops or when drug-resistant strains are present, but they are less effective, have more side effects, and require longer treatment. Drug-susceptible infections are treated with a combination of four first-line drugs for 4 or 6 months. The 6-month HRZE regimen (isoniazid, rifapentine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) is taken daily for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifapentine for four months, and is highly effective when followed properly. The 4-month HMPZ regimen has moderate evidence of effectiveness but has several contraindications. If first-line treatment fails, a drug susceptibility test (DST) is used to guide second-line regimens, which historically required long (18–24 months) and costly treatments, often leading to incomplete courses. As of 2025, WHO recommends two 6-month and two 9-month regimens for drug-resistant TB using oral second-line drugs, all with good evidence of effectiveness. The 6-month regimens are BPaLM and BDLLfx. Adherence to treatment is challenging due to the need for daily medication over long periods, unpleasant side effects, and the rapid improvement in symptoms that may lead patients to discontinue treatment prematurely. In areas without strong public health systems, treatment is expensive. Failure to complete treatment can lead to drug-resistant TB. Public health bodies recommend support during treatment, including directly observed therapy (a healthcare worker watches the patient take medication, in person or online), case management, digital monitoring, health education, counseling, and community support. TB is generally curable with prompt and appropriate treatment but can be fatal if untreated. Without treatment, about two-thirds of people with TB will die within three years of diagnosis. Progression from latent infection to active TB occurs when the bacteria overcome immune defenses and multiply; in 1–5% of cases, this happens soon after infection, but in most cases, a latent infection develops without symptoms. Over a lifetime, 5–10% of latent cases progress to active TB, often years after initial infection. The risk of reactivation increases when the immune system weakens, such as from certain medications or HIV co-infection. In people co-infected with HIV and TB, the risk of reactivation rises to 10% per year, and HIV co-infection significantly worsens TB prognosis, leading to higher mortality and poorer treatment outcomes.

Tuberculosis (TB) is a disease with a significant global burden, affecting approximately one-quarter of the world's population, with new infections occurring in about 11 million people annually. Most TB infections do not lead to disease, with 90–95% remaining asymptomatic, and about two-thirds of untreated individuals die from the disease within three years of diagnosis. Progression from latent TB infection to active disease occurs when the bacteria overcome immune defenses and multiply, happening in 1–5% of cases shortly after initial infection, though in most cases, a latent infection develops without symptoms. Over a lifetime, 5–10% of latent infections reactivate, often years later. The risk of reactivation increases when the immune system is weakened, such as by certain drug treatments or HIV co-infection, with people co-infected with M. tuberculosis and HIV facing a 10% annual reactivation risk. HIV significantly worsens TB prognosis, increasing susceptibility to active TB and leading to higher mortality and poorer treatment outcomes; people with HIV are 12 times more likely to develop TB than those without HIV, and TB is the leading cause of death among them. TB has been documented throughout history, with Hippocrates describing phthisis around 400 BCE and references in ancient Indian texts like the Vedas (1500–1200 BCE), and early evidence found in prehistoric human remains dating back to the early Neolithic era (10,000–11,000 years ago). Phylogenetic analysis shows the TB bacterium adapted to humans in Africa around 70,000 years ago and spread globally with human migration. TB disproportionately affects low-income populations and countries due to factors like poverty, poor living conditions, malnutrition, and limited healthcare access, with the highest burden in low- and middle-income countries, particularly in the WHO South-East Asia, African, and Western Pacific regions. The majority of new cases occur in 30 high-burden countries, including Bangladesh, China, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, and the Philippines. India has an estimated 40% infection rate, attributed to poverty, malnutrition, overcrowding, and stigma, with incidence decreasing from nearly 300 per 100,000 in 2010 to 200 in 2023. Indonesia reports about one million cases and 134,000 deaths annually, with rising incidence linked to the COVID-19 pandemic; China’s incidence has declined from 67 to 40 per 100,000 between 2010 and 2023, though higher risks exist in poorer regions like Xinjiang and Tibet. The Philippines accounts for 6.8% of global TB cases, with incidence rising from 520 to 625 per 100,000 between 2007 and 2024, driven by poverty, overcrowding, and health inequities. Lesotho has a high incidence of 664 per 100,000 in 2023, down from 1,184 in 2010, but remains among the highest globally, due to a 23% HIV prevalence, lack of funding, geographic challenges, and poor treatment adherence. TB has been known by various names, including phthisis, consumption, tabes, and "the great white plague," and was historically associated with artistic talent, influencing figures like Keats, Shelley, Chopin, and Dostoevsky. It has also been linked to cultural myths, such as in 19th century New England where TB was believed to be transmitted by vampires. Some countries historically involuntarily detained or treated TB patients, and today many require TB notifications and negative TB tests for visas. The World Health Organization has promoted strategies including DOTS (launched in 1995) and the Stop TB Strategy (2006–2014), which aimed to halt TB incidence and address drug resistance and HIV co-infection, followed by the End TB Strategy (2014), setting targets for a 90% reduction in TB deaths and 80% reduction in incidence by 2030, with additional goals for prevention and eliminating catastrophic costs by 2020. In 2012, the WHO, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and U.S. government introduced the Xpert MTB/RIF test, a rapid molecular diagnostic tool that provides results in about two hours, detecting TB and rifampicin resistance simultaneously. TB stigma, reported by 42–82% of affected individuals, leads to social exclusion, delayed diagnosis, poor treatment adherence, and transmission. Stigma stems from misconceptions about transmissibility, poverty, or HIV/AIDS, and may result in bans from public gatherings or job loss, especially in India. The End TB Strategy identifies four key research areas: diagnostics, active TB treatment, latent TB treatment, and vaccines. Diagnostics remain slow and expensive, especially for latent or extrapulmonary infections, and improvements are needed through faster, blood-based molecular tests and portable point-of-care devices. Treatment typically involves long-term daily drug regimens, which can lead to non-adherence; shorter, simpler regimens and new drugs are needed to improve outcomes. Despite the existence of the BCG vaccine since over a century ago, it remains the only licensed vaccine with highly variable effectiveness, and a candidate, MVA85A, failed in 2019 clinical trials, highlighting the urgent need for better vaccines.

Before starting a course of treatment, shorter and simpler treatment regimens, along with the introduction of new drugs, have the potential to improve adherence and thus improve outcomes.[141] Research can lead to improvements in two key areas: the treatment of active tuberculosis, including both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant strains, through safer, easier, and shorter regimens that would enhance availability and adherence and lead to better outcomes; and the treatment and elimination of latent TB infection to prevent its progression to active disease, where improved regimens would also result in better outcomes.[141] However, there is limited evidence that improved treatment regimens actually improve outcomes, and it will also be necessary to enhance health literacy and support structures for individuals with TB.[244] Despite being originally developed over a century ago,[a] as of 2025[update], BCG remains the only vaccine licensed for use, although it has highly variable effectiveness.[245] A promising vaccine candidate, MVA85A, failed in 2019 to show effectiveness in clinical trials.[246] There is an urgent need for improved vaccines that could be effective both before exposure to TB and after exposure.[141] Fundamental research must continue into the interaction between the bacterium and its human host,[247] the detailed chain of steps leading to TB transmission,[248] and the social and political barriers to effective implementation of the elimination strategy.[249] Members of the genus Mycobacterium infect various animals, including birds,[250] fish,[251] and reptiles,[252] but the species Mycobacterium tuberculosis is rarely found in wild animals.[253] An effort to eradicate bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis from cattle and deer herds in New Zealand has been relatively successful.[254] Efforts in Great Britain have been less successful.[255][256] As of 2015[update], tuberculosis is widespread among captive elephants in the US, believed to have originally been acquired from humans through a process called reverse zoonosis; because the disease can spread through the air and infect both humans and animals, it poses a public health concern in circuses and zoos.[257][258]
